metadata.title: Claude, Flashcards.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Teardown of the 'flashcards skill' — take apart the naming misdirection, explain the actual mechanism (one file, read top to bottom before Claude starts), name the trade-off (structure at the expense of range), and land the carry-out that a skill is a specification being enforced, not new model knowledge.
metadata.anchor_pair: B03 -> B06 (flashcards' single SKILL.md: planted, then returned to)

beats.narration_text: The name 'flashcards skill' does a bit of misdirection. You hear it and picture Claude picking up an ability. Here's what's actually happening: Claude gets handed a file of instructions. 'Flashcards' is what the file is named. Let's open it.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Claude learned to make flashcards from that skill.', hesitates on 'learned', corrects to 'was given', lands the real question

props.text:
Claude learned to make
flashcards from that skill.
What is a skill?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('learned' -> 'was given') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Say 'Claude has a flashcards skill' out loud and it lands like a capability upgrade — as if the model went off, studied quiz-writing, and came back with new wiring. That reading is intuitive. It's also wrong.

Test the intuition: delete the folder. If Claude had actually learned something, deletion would erase it. Nothing erases. Claude still writes flashcards the same way it always could — it just stops running that specific routine on top.

Here's the mechanism, stripped: a skill is one file. The flashcards skill is a folder holding a single SKILL.md — plain-language instructions for turning source material into prompt-and-answer cards. Claude reads that file before it starts. That's the whole payload.

The execution model is deliberately dumb: top to bottom, step by step, in the order the file lists them. No branching unless the file itself says branch. That choice trades cleverness for reproducibility.

So a skill is a specification, not a power. The payoff is consistency: same structure, every card, one prompt, one answer, every run. The cost is generality — anything outside the written steps and Claude is off the map. They optimized for structure at the expense of range.

So the flashcards skill never taught Claude anything. What it guarantees is repetition: every run, same file, same prompt-and-answer structure. That's not learning. That's a specification being enforced — and it's the whole trick.

beats.narration_text: Neither output proves what you'd think. Clean cards don't mean Claude understood the material — a specification can be followed to the letter on a topic the model never really grasped. Messy cards don't mean the skill is broken — sometimes the material just doesn't fit the file's shape.
A skill doesn't teach Claude anything. It's a file of steps Claude reads before it starts. Every card set comes out with the same structure — because the structure is written down, not learned.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste straight into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — it'll write you a real specification you can use tomorrow. Go deeper: what would break if two people wrote SKILL.md files for the same task and Claude ran both?

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to turn one of my repeatable tasks into a SKILL.md — a plain-language, ordered specification another AI could follow. Help me pick a task: any document I produce roughly the same way every time (a status update, a lesson plan, a code review, a customer reply). Ask me three sharp questions to pin down the exact inputs, the ordered steps, and how I know it's done. Then write the SKILL.md — no branches unless a step demands one — read it back to me, and walk me through exactly what you'd do on a fresh input before doing it.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: if two people wrote SKILL.md files for the same task and Claude ran both, what would come out different — and what does that tell you about where the specification really lives: in the file, or in the person who wrote it?
